name: Pedro Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit counter frames and timber partitions at the Station Road shop row. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and have enough site years to finish an ordinary frame, although I still ask the lead on an unusual load-bearing wall. My partner Ines does catering shifts when events are booked, and our grown children are settled elsewhere. The builder's rate is low, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and only a few other crews work within my bus route. I use an AI assistant every morning to sort my cutting notes and check a supplier catalogue, then measure the site myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little smarter software can save us a wrong trip to the timber yard. It cannot turn a short week into a full wage, so I'd keep looking at the job board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pleased when the tool helps, but our money is tight before any AI shock. Ines's catering work comes and goes, and three weeks of savings would disappear if this shop row paused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the counters and checking my AI lists against the actual bays. In the first year I'll use the usual supplier tool, ask foreman Leon when the next unit starts and take any paid local partition work that follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about small improvements and anxious about paid hours. A tidy list is useful only if there is a job to take it to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the list save a trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It reminded me that the end unit needs longer brackets, which I checked against the wall before ordering. The right box came in one delivery instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your adult children cover a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would probably offer a meal, but I don't want their wages in our budget. Ines and I need steady paid weeks, not a quiet transfer from the children.

say: I'd welcome **fewer timber-yard trips** from checked software.
I'd remind the crew **full wages** depend on booked work.
think: Our **three-week reserve** is already exposed to a site pause.
Ines's **event catering** cannot reliably cover my low site wage.
do: Keep fitting **shop counters** and checking AI lists against bays.
Ask Leon for the **next unit date** and accept paid local partition work.
feel: **Curious and anxious** about tools and the paid-hours board.
S0.quote: A tidy list is useful only if there is a job to take it to.
fieldNote: Pedro's daily AI habit saved a **bracket delivery**, but he measures the real wall before ordering.
Irregular catering work and a **three-week reserve** keep income worry alive even in a mild picture.

steps.text: Keep taking paid counter-framing shifts at Station Road
Use AI cutting lists with site measurements each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying software could move faster, and I'd volunteer to run a real partition order through it. I would ask the buyer to show where the corrected quantities go when a wall moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer office workers might mean the next shop fitout is booked differently or late. I can learn the system quickly, but a fast screen cannot replace two weeks of wages if the foreman has no new unit for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare one digital order with the timber delivered for the end unit and keep taking paid shifts. If the next shop opening slides a week, I'll apply to the two reachable contractors and stop our Saturday bakery visit until the hours return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the trial and anxious about the calendar. I'd rather make a call early than wait until the savings tin is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a good trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corrected wall dimensions must produce the right boards, not just a neat invoice. I would count every piece when the lorry comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the Saturday bakery visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a small pleasure Ines and I share, and cutting it saves something without touching rent or bus fares. We can bring it back when paid weeks return.

say: I'd volunteer for a **real partition order** through the new screen.
I'd ask how **changed wall dimensions** reach the supplier.
think: Office changes could delay the **next shop fitout**.
Fast tool learning cannot replace **missing paid weeks** with our small reserve.
do: Compare a **digital order** with delivered timber.
Keep **paid shifts** and apply after a one-week shop delay.
Pause **Saturday bakery visits** until full hours return.
feel: **Interested in testing**, anxious about the shop calendar.
S1.quote: I can learn the system quickly, but a fast screen cannot replace two weeks of wages if the foreman has no new unit for us.
fieldNote: Pedro tests AI against **moved walls** and real boards, drawing on daily use without trusting an invoice alone.
His application trigger is **one delayed week**, and the first cut is a small shared outing.

steps.text: Trial the AI ordering screen on the end-unit partition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 might do the buying and drawings, but robots that can set partitions come around 2031. I would ask the firm to show one robot build an awkward shop corner before it changes anyone's shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when the office work changes and sixty-three when a robot might take my fitting hours. Ines's event shifts and our three-week reserve won't pay rent for long if I lose this low wage, whatever the machine saves the builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll test the digital layout checker with Leon and gather my signed room sheets. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid fitout work, apply to the two local repair firms if shifts fall, and ask the trade school about a paid maintenance apprenticeship; I'd enrol only if the placement is reachable and covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the short lead, though I still want to learn the checker. Knowing a clever tool may help before 2031 and still leave me searching when the robot can do the wall itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid repairs might give me another run of work while I learn a second set of jobs. I don't think maintenance will be safe forever once robots can handle hands-on tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot to stay ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not spend our three-week buffer on a machine with no confirmed customers. I'd rather ask for a paid apprenticeship than gamble the rent.

say: I'd separate **2028 drawings** from the 2031 robots that could set whole shop partitions.
I'd require an **awkward-corner trial** before shifts change.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could remove my paid partition work.
Our **three-week savings** and event income cannot carry rent for long.
do: Test the **layout checker** and collect signed room sheets.
Keep **paid fitout shifts** in 2029 and apply if hours fall.
Enrol in **paid maintenance training** only with reachable work.
feel: **Frightened**, yet willing to learn and apply for paid work.
S2.quote: I would not spend our three-week buffer on a machine with no confirmed customers.
fieldNote: Pedro distinguishes present **digital layout help** from later hands-on robot replacement.
He rejects buying a robot with **rent money** and makes apprenticeship conditional on paid reachable work.

steps.text: Test the digital layout checker on an actual shop corner
Keep taking paid fitout shifts in 2029
Apply to two local repair firms if site hours fall
Enrol in maintenance training only with a paid reachable placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for builders to test machines on working sites and for apprentices to learn the trade while being paid. I would ask for the actual next-job list, not a story about plenty of future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots might set the shop partitions. More years help, but low pay and Ines's uneven shifts make retirement by then an uncertain guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid shop work and using checked AI layouts on the current rooms. In 2032 I'd still fit partitions if shifts exist, ask Leon for a six-month work list and apply to local contractors if a fortnight is blank; after full months I'd try to put a little into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less hurried by technology, but not safe from our usual income gaps. A five-year warning is only worth what the pay packets inside it are worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make training worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid placement with a local employer and work I can do without a long commute. I would enrol in that, not in an expensive certificate chosen from a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small amount after a full month, but some months the shop row stops early. I won't call a wish to save a plan until the wage has arrived.

say: I'd ask for **working-site trials** and paid apprenticeships.
I'd demand an **actual job list** over the five-year lead.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots may meet an uncertain retirement budget.
Low pay and **uneven catering** mean extra years may bring little saving.
do: Keep **paid shop work** and checked AI layouts.
Fit **partitions in 2032** if paid shifts remain.
Apply locally after a **blank fortnight** and save only after full months.
feel: Less **hurried by robots**, still exposed to ordinary wage gaps.
S3.quote: I won't call a wish to save a plan until the wage has arrived.
fieldNote: Pedro's **five-year warning** remains tied to paid work rather than an assumed retirement date.
He will save only after **full paid months** and considers training only with a local paid placement.

steps.text: Keep taking paid partition shifts in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to teach the younger ones how to square a frame and check what any new machine does on site. I would still ask the foreman about next week's paid work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can set partitions. I may still need paid repairs then, because a low wage and three weeks saved today give me no honest retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting frames while my hands hold up and using AI for checked lists on paid jobs. In 2037 I'd take lighter paid repairs if needed, and Ines and I would count real income and bills before I stopped looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a robot that distant, but anxious about the next slow catering month. Ten years on a card cannot buy groceries tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and bills. I would rather ask them to eat with us than turn their wages into our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make next year easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady run of paid shop units and a slightly better rate would help more than any prediction. Then we could add a fourth week to the savings tin.

say: I'd use the decade to **teach frame checks** on working sites.
I'd ask about **next week's pay** before worrying about 2039.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid repairs may still be necessary.
At **seventy-one**, low wages and thin savings leave retirement uncertain.
do: Keep **paid frame fitting** and checked AI lists.
Take **lighter repairs in 2037** if wages are needed.
Count **income and bills** with Ines before leaving work.
feel: **Anxious about current pay**, calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: Ten years on a card cannot buy groceries tonight.
fieldNote: Pedro retains **daily AI use** while treating the 2039 robot date as distant from present bills.
He expects **paid repairs** if necessary in later life and does not treat grown children as income.

steps.text: Keep taking paid frame-fitting shifts while fit
Use checked AI lists on current paid jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because hands-on robots could reach partitions by sixty-three while we have only three weeks saved. A paid local apprenticeship, honest job dates and a real robot trial would help me keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens when the digital list is right but the old wall is crooked. The worker still has to make a frame fit the room someone actually lives in.

headlineQuote: The worker still has to make a frame fit the room someone actually lives in.
portrait: Pedro is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level shop-fitout experience.
His low wage, Ines's uneven catering shifts and **three weeks saved** make delays costly.
He uses **AI every day**, checking supplier lists against real walls and delivered boards.
He seeks **paid local training** while retaining fitting work and rejecting an unaffordable robot purchase.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could remove his partition-fitting wage by the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid local apprenticeship**, clear job dates and a real site trial.
